topic: Back to sport after ACL reconstruction: why it takes time

slides.headline: ACL rehab: why patience pays off
slides.sub: Feeling good isn't the same as ready. Here's what return to sport involves.

slides.title: The graft needs time
slides.body: A new ACL graft keeps remodelling for many months after surgery. The knee can feel fine well before it's ready for cutting, jumping and contact. Your surgeon's protocol sets the early boundaries.

slides.title: Strength before speed
slides.body: Quad and hamstring strength often lag behind for longer than people expect. Rehab usually builds strength first, then running, then jumping and landing, then change of direction.

slides.title: Testing, not guessing
slides.body: Rather than a date on the calendar, return decisions often use strength tests, hop tests and sport-specific drills compared with the other leg. Confidence in the knee matters too.

slides.title: Why rushing rarely pays
slides.body: Research suggests returning to pivoting sport too early is linked with a higher chance of reinjury. A longer, well-planned build-up is usually a better bet than a quick comeback.

slides.title: Keep the motivation going
slides.body: Set small goals, track your strength numbers and train with your team where it's appropriate. Many people find the mental side of the comeback as big as the physical side.

slides.headline: Planning your return to sport?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios work alongside your surgeon's protocol, with testing to guide each step back to sport. Book online, link in bio.

caption:
Knee feels great, so why can't you play yet? It's the most common question in ACL rehab.

After a reconstruction, the graft keeps remodelling for many months, and strength in the quads and hamstrings often takes longer to return than people expect. Feeling good isn't the same as being ready for cutting, jumping and contact.

That's why return decisions usually rely on strength and hop testing and sport-specific drills rather than a date on the calendar, always alongside your surgeon's protocol. Research suggests a patient build-up lowers the chance of reinjury.
